title: Distant opposition
summary: Use opposition to reach key squares, protect your pawns and prevent the opposing king from entering; choose when to follow, wait or outflank.
part.distant.title: Distant opposition
part.distant.summary: With the kings far apart, take the opposition from afar. With every step of the other king, it turns into direct opposition.
step.t_lesson: In this lesson you will learn to use opposition to reach key squares, stop the enemy king from getting in and choose the moment to wait or to go round. It assumes you already know direct opposition, key squares, promotion and stalemate. First identify the goal; then choose the technique. The key squares of the g3-pawn are f5, g5 and h5. Which first move prepares the white king’s access to those squares?
step.t_lesson.hint1: Put the kings on the same file and count the squares between them.
step.t_lesson.hint2: With an odd number of squares between the kings and the other side to move, the opposition is yours.
step.intro:
Key squares are squares which, once the king occupies them, guarantee the pawn’s promotion against the best defence. For the g3-pawn they are f5, g5 and h5. The problem is reaching one of them without letting the black king block the way.

To know who has the opposition, with the kings on the same file (or the same rank), count the empty squares between them. If the number is odd (one, three or five) and it is the opponent’s turn, the side that has just moved has the opposition. With one square between the kings the opposition is direct; with three or five it is distant.

In this position, 1.Ke4 leaves e5, e6 and e7 between the kings, with Black to move. After 1...Kf7, 2.Kf5 reaches a key square. If Black retreats to f8, the plan is the same: 1.Ke4 Kf8 2.Kf5!, and the white king occupies the key square before the pawn advances. Counting only helps when it takes the king to the square it needs; the pawns and the squares they control count too.

{{Capablanca|jose-raul-capablanca}} states the same rule the other way round: with an even number of squares between the kings, the side to move can take the opposition.
step.d_distant: Watch distant opposition turn into direct opposition, one step at a time.
step.d_distant.m1: 1.Ke4! The white king stands on the black king’s file, with three squares between them, e5, e6 and e7, and Black to move. By the counting rule, the distant opposition belongs to White.
step.d_distant.m2: 1...Kf7. The black king cannot pass; it leaves the e-file for f7, on its way to g6, in front of the pawn. If White is careless and plays the natural 2.g4?, Black draws with 2...Kg6! The black king stands in front of the pawn on g6, and the white king can no longer reach a key square.
step.d_distant.m3: 2.Kf5! The white king moves to the new file and stands in front of the black king, one square between them: this is direct opposition. Moreover, f5 is already a key square of the g3-pawn. It is the only winning move.
step.d_distant.m4: 2...Kg7. The black king gives way again, now to the g-file, and tries to get back in front of the pawn. Black has a resource here too: if White plays the natural 3.g4?, Black draws with 3...Kf7!
step.d_distant.m5: 3.Kg5! The white king stands in front again, on another key square; it is the only winning move. From here the pawn queens.
step.convert: Play White and find the best move. This time the black king answers differently.
step.convert.hint:
Before advancing the pawn, look for a king square that leaves an odd number of squares between the kings. Then see whether you can shorten the distance or reach a key square.

These do not work either:

At move 1
The king needs to gain space before the pawn advances.
If White played 1.Ke3?, Black would reply 1...Ke7 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.Ke3 Ke7 2.g4 Ke6.
If White played 1.g4?, Black would reply 1...Kd7 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.g4 Kd7 2.g5 Kd6.

At move 2
Here, advancing to the available key square is valid; leaving the struggle or spending the reserve allows a blockade.
If White played 2.Kf4?, Black would reply 2...Kf6 and hold the draw. The line would be 2.Kf4 Kf6 3.g4 Kg6.
If White played 2.g4?, Black would reply 2...Ke6 and hold the draw. The line would be 2.g4 Ke6 3.g5 Ke7.

At move 3
The king must reach the key square before releasing the pawn.
If White played 3.g4?, Black would reply 3...Kg6 and hold the draw. The line would be 3.g4 Kg6 4.g5 Kxg5.
step.convert.done:
That is how to convert: the king gained space before the pawn advanced, and the distant opposition opened the way to a key square. After 1...Ke7, both 2.Ke5, with direct opposition and Black to move, and 2.Kf5, which already stands on a key square, win.

The main line is 1.Ke4 Ke7 2.Ke5 Kf7 3.Kf5.
2.Kf5 also works.
part.diagonal.title: Diagonal opposition
part.diagonal.summary: When the file is out of reach, the opposition also works along a diagonal.
step.t_diagonal: The black king watches the key squares of the e3-pawn. The natural 1.Ke4 looks good, but it is not. Which square leaves the black king without a good reply?
step.t_diagonal.hint1: The kings need not be on the same file: a diagonal works too, with one square between them.
step.t_diagonal.hint2: After coming in along the diagonal, wherever the black king goes, look to face him again, from any side.
step.diagonal: Until now the kings were on the same file. Now they are not, and the link between them is the diagonal. 1.Ke4 looks natural, but after 1...Ke6 it is the black king that has the direct opposition, and the e3-pawn does not get through. The correct entry is 1.Kf4: the kings stand on the f4-e5-d6 diagonal, with one square between them and Black to move. After 1.Kf4 Ke6, the white king answers with 2.Ke4!, face to face, and Black has to give way. From there the white king answers every move by keeping one square between the kings, on the same file or the same rank.
step.d_diagonal: Watch the diagonal turn into direct opposition.
step.d_diagonal.m1: 1.Kf4. Kings on the diagonal f4, e5, d6, one square in between, and Black to move.
step.d_diagonal.m2: 1...Ke6. The black king moves in front of the pawn to block the e-file. If White played the natural 2.e4?, Black would draw with 2...Kf6! With f5 between the kings and White to move, the direct opposition would pass to Black.
step.d_diagonal.m3: 2.Ke4! The only winning move: the kings stand face to face on the e-file, one square apart, and Black is to move. That is the direct opposition.
step.d_diagonal.m4: 2...Kd6. The black king has to give way and goes to d6, from where it still guards d5 and e5; the f5-square is left free.
step.d_diagonal.m5: 3.Kf5. The key square that was left free. With the king here, the e3-pawn queens.
step.diagonalMove: Play White and find the best move. The black king watches the key squares of the e3-pawn.
step.diagonalMove.hint:
First look for diagonal opposition. After the reply, identify the rank or file on which your king can prevent the opposing king from approaching and reach a key square.

These do not work either:

At move 1
The diagonal entry prepares useful opposition; the pawn advance and direct approach give the defender the time it needs.
If White played 1.e4?, Black would reply 1...Ke5 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.e4 Ke5 2.Ke2 Kxe4.
If White played 1.Ke4?, Black would reply 1...Ke6 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.Ke4 Ke6 2.Kd3 Kd5.

At move 2
The key square along the rank is decisive; a pawn check cannot replace the king’s position.
If White played 2.e4+?, Black would reply 2...Ke6 and hold the draw. The line would be 2.e4+ Ke6 3.e5 Kd7.
step.diagonalMove.done:
The right entry: 1.Kf4 took the opposition along the diagonal and, after 1...Kd5, 2.Kf5 reached a key square, with the kings on the same rank and e5 between them.

The main line is 1.Kf4 Kd5 2.Kf5.
part.defend.title: In defence
part.defend.summary: The defender uses the same rule. He takes the opposition from afar, even by stepping back, and follows the attacking king.
step.t_carlsenSo: Now a real game, from the defender's side. {{Stavanger|stavanger}}, 2017, {{Norway Chess|norway-chess}}: {{Magnus Carlsen|magnus-carlsen}}, with White, against {{Wesley So|wesley-so}}. The knights came off on move 53, and So was a pawn down, two white pawns against one. The white king wants to get in and capture the h6-pawn. Only one move draws. Which one?
step.t_carlsenSo.hint1: Count the squares between the kings on the f-file.
step.t_carlsenSo.hint2: Two squares in between is an even number: on the move, you can make it odd, even by stepping back.
step.defend:
At {{Norway Chess|norway-chess}} in {{Stavanger|stavanger}} in 2017, {{Magnus Carlsen|magnus-carlsen}}, with White, faced {{Wesley So|wesley-so}}, with Black. After the knights were exchanged on move 53, So was a pawn down and had to defend the h6-pawn. The black king is on f6; the white king, on f3.

Opposition also serves the side with less material. The defending king wants to stop the attacking king from gaining space to support the pawns or attack h6.

In the game, 55...Kf7! left f4, f5 and f6 between the kings, with White to move. When the white king changed file, So followed: 56.Ke3 Ke7 57.Kd3 Kd7. After 58.Kc4, 58...Ke6 went back towards the pawns: defending does not require keeping the same distance throughout.

Now White has a single pawn, on g3, and the black king must deny f5, g5 and h5. The premature-approach example starts with the black king on f6 and White’s on f3. After 1.Kf4 Kg6 2.Kg4, White has the opposition and wins: the black king controls the squares ahead, but has to move and, by giving way on one side, lets the white king in on the other.

What to do: retreat to f7, far enough to answer the white king’s advance. After 1...Kf7 2.Ke4, Black replies 2...Ke6, face to face, or 2...Kg6, and the white king does not get in.
step.d_carlsenSo: The moves of the game. For the white king’s first three steps, So keeps his king on the white king’s file, with three squares between them.
step.d_carlsenSo.m1: 55...Kf7! He steps back and takes the distant opposition: f4, f5 and f6 in between, and White to move.
step.d_carlsenSo.m2: 56.Ke3. {{Carlsen|magnus-carlsen}} changes file, trying to get in along the e-file.
step.d_carlsenSo.m3: 56...Ke7! So changes file with him: three squares in between again, now on the e-file.
step.d_carlsenSo.m4: 57.Kd3. {{Carlsen|magnus-carlsen}} tries the d-file. If So does not follow now, he loses: 57...Kd7 is again the only move.
step.d_carlsenSo.m5: 57...Kd7! Facing him again, from afar. The white king moves, but gains no ground.
step.d_carlsenSo.m6: 58.Kc4. {{Carlsen|magnus-carlsen}} goes up the c-file, to come in on the queenside.
step.d_carlsenSo.m7: 58...Ke6! The black king comes back close to the pawns, and the white king has no way in. The game was drawn on move 63.
step.defendMove: Play Black and find the best move. Now White has a single pawn, on g3.
step.defendMove.hint:
Defending may require a retreat. Look for a square on the white king’s file that leaves an odd number of squares between the kings and White to move. If the pawn advances, check its key squares again.

These do not work either:

At move 1
The defence must retreat to the correct distance. Moving closer or retreating too far lets the white king gain ground.
If Black played 1...Kf6?, White would reply 2.Kf4 and win. The line would be 1...Kf6 2.Kf4 Kg6 3.Kg4.
If Black played 1...Kf8?, White would reply 2.Kf4 and win. The line would be 1...Kf8 2.Kf4 Kf7 3.Kg5.

At move 2
The opposition must adapt to the white king’s new file. There is more than one defence, but not every nearby square works.
If Black played 2...Kf6?, White would reply 3.Kf4 and win. The line would be 2...Kf6 3.Kf4 Kg6 4.Kg4.
If Black played 2...Kg7?, White would reply 3.Kf5 and win. The line would be 2...Kg7 3.Kf5 Kh6 4.g4.

At move 3
After the pawn advance, occupying the key square matters more than keeping the previous distance.
If Black played 3...Kf7?, White would reply 4.Kf5 and win. The line would be 3...Kf7 4.Kf5 Kg7 5.Kg5.
step.defendMove.done:
A sound defence: 1...Kf7 left f4, f5 and f6 between the kings, with White to move, and followed the change of file. After 3.g4 the key squares become f6, g6 and h6, and 3...Kf6 occupies one of them. 2...Kg6 also draws, because the black king still watches f5, g5 and h5.

The main line is 1...Kf7 2.Ke4 Ke6 3.g4 Kf6.
2...Kg6 also works.
At the third decision, 3...Kf6 occupies the square needed for the defense.
part.lateral.title: Lateral opposition
part.lateral.summary: The opposition also works along a rank, near and far, in attack and in defence.
step.t_euwe: Now the kings face each other on the same rank. In The Hague in 1928, the World Amateur Championship was held alongside the Olympiad as a separate individual competition. In this game, {{Max Euwe|max-euwe}} had White against {{Norman Whitaker|norman-whitaker}}. The rooks were exchanged on move 47, leaving each side with one pawn. The struggle is to reach the opposing pawn first: your king is heading for a5, while the black king threatens to reach c2. Only one move wins. Which move is it?
step.t_euwe.hint1: The kings can also face each other on the same rank.
step.t_euwe.hint2: Count the squares between the kings on the fifth rank after your move.
step.lateral: So far the kings faced each other head on or along a diagonal; {{Euwe|max-euwe}} used the rank. He played 49.Kb5, attacking the a5-pawn and placing the kings on the fifth rank with three squares between them and Black to move. This is distant opposition along the rank. Notice the order: first reach a useful rank, then follow the opposing king’s changes without abandoning your pawns. In the line, after capturing a5, the white king returns towards the c2-pawn. Following the other king makes sense only if that route also protects your own pawns.
step.d_euwe: The moves of the game: {{Euwe|max-euwe}} always stays on the black king's rank.
step.d_euwe.m1: 49.Kb5! The only winning move. Kings on b5 and f5, three squares in between, and Black to move.
step.d_euwe.m3: 50.Kxa5! The pawn falls, and the kings again have three squares in between, a5 and e5, with Black to move.
step.d_euwe.m4: 50...Kd4. He goes further down and threatens 51...Kc3, attacking the c2-pawn.
step.d_euwe.m5: 51.Kb4! Kings on b4 and d4, one square in between, and Black to move: lateral opposition, and c3 is shut to him.
step.d_euwe.m6: 51...Kd5. With no way through c3, he steps back. Every move loses: the white king is already in front of the pawn.
step.d_euwe.m7: 52.Kb5. The white king goes up in front of the pawn, towards b6 and c6. {{Euwe|max-euwe}} went on with 53.c4, 54.Kb6 and 55.Kc6, and the game ended there, a win for White.
step.lateralDefend: Play Black and find the best move. The white king wants to support the d2-pawn.
step.lateralDefend.hint:
Count the distance along the rank. Follow the white king’s descent without allowing it to reach the key squares before you.

These do not work either:

At move 1
The defending king needs to reach the same rank in time.
If Black played 1...Ke7?, White would reply 2.Kb5 and win. The line would be 1...Ke7 2.Kb5 Kd6 3.Kc4.
If Black played 1...Kf6?, White would reply 2.Kb5 and win. The line would be 1...Kf6 2.Kb5 Ke6 3.Kc5.

At move 2
Lateral opposition prevents access to the key squares; a difference of one square can open the route.
If Black played 2...Kd6?, White would reply 3.Kc4 and win. The line would be 2...Kd6 3.Kc4 Kc6 4.d3.
If Black played 2...Ke5?, White would reply 3.Kc5 and win. The line would be 2...Ke5 3.Kc5 Kf5 4.d4.

At move 3
Following along the rank keeps a barrier between the attacking king and the decisive squares.
If Black played 3...Kd6?, White would reply 4.Kc4 and win. The line would be 3...Kd6 4.Kc4 Kc6 5.d3.
If Black played 3...Ke4?, White would reply 4.Kc4 and win. The line would be 3...Ke4 4.Kc4 Ke5 5.Kc5.
step.lateralDefend.done:
Defence along the rank: lateral opposition maintained a barrier in front of the decisive squares. Following along the rank can require retreating before facing the king.

The main line is 1...Ke6 2.Kb5 Kd5 3.Kb4 Kd4.
The replies 2...Kd5 and 3...Kd4 follow the change of rank and maintain the barrier.
part.capablanca.title: Capablanca's example
part.capablanca.summary: With blocked pawns on both wings, obtain opposition before choosing the route in.
step.t_capablanca: Locked pawns on both sides and the kings far apart. Whoever reaches an enemy pawn first wins. Think: which white king move makes sure of getting there first?
step.t_capablanca.hint1: Count the squares between the kings on the e-file. With an even number, the side to move can take the opposition.
step.t_capablanca.hint2: Six squares in between and your move: after your move an odd number must be left.
step.capablanca: Now there are pawns on both sides, and the target is not queening: it is the other side's pawn. This is the example {{Capablanca|jose-raul-capablanca}} chose, in Chess Fundamentals, to show the value of the opposition. Each side has two blocked pawns, b4 against b5 and h4 against h5, and the kings are on e1 and e8, with six squares between them. An even number: whoever is to move takes the opposition, and whoever takes the opposition wins, because he reaches the other side's pawn first. 1.Ke2 is the only move that wins. After 1.Ke2 Ke7, only 2.Ke3! keeps the opposition: three squares remain between the kings, e4, e5 and e6, and Black is to move.
step.d_capablanca: Watch distant opposition become direct. The preparation for outflanking will be examined in the next section.
step.d_capablanca.m1: 1.Ke2. Five squares in between, and Black to move.
step.d_capablanca.m2: 1...Ke7. The black king advances down the e-file, aiming to shorten the distance and take the opposition itself. If White answered 2.Kd3?, leaving the file, Black would draw with 2...Kf6.
step.d_capablanca.m3: 2.Ke3! It is the only winning move: there are three squares between the kings, e4, e5 and e6, and Black is to move again.
step.d_capablanca.m4: 2...Ke6. The black king advances again and leaves only two squares between the kings, with White to move. Going diagonally would be natural, but 3.Kd4? Kd6! or 3.Kf4? Kf6! would give Black the direct opposition, with White to move, and it would be a draw.
step.d_capablanca.m5: 3.Ke4! Direct opposition, with one square between the kings and Black to move; now Black has to leave the file.
step.capablancaMove: Play White and find the best move. This time the black king leaves the file on its very first move.
step.capablancaMove.hint:
First consider who will have to give way on the kings’ file. If the opposing king changes file, compare a diagonal step with approaching in a straight line: what matters is the opposition after its reply.

These do not work either:

At move 1
The first step must establish distant opposition before choosing a wing.
If White played 1.Kd2?, Black would reply 1...Kf7 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.Kd2 Kf7 2.Kc3 Ke6.
If White played 1.Kf2?, Black would reply 1...Kd7 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.Kf2 Kd7 2.Ke3 Ke7.

At move 2
The black king’s change of file requires recalculating the opposition after its reply.
If White played 2.Ke3?, Black would reply 2...Ke7 and hold the draw. The line would be 2.Ke3 Ke7 3.Kd3 Kf6.
If White played 2.Kf3?, Black would reply 2...Kf7 and hold the draw. The line would be 2.Kf3 Kf7 3.Ke3 Ke7.

At move 3
After the lateral waiting move, it is time to return to the file at the correct distance.
If White played 3.Kd4?, Black would reply 3...Kd6 and hold the draw. The line would be 3.Kd4 Kd6 4.Ke4 Ke6.
If White played 3.Ke4?, Black would reply 3...Ke6 and hold the draw. The line would be 3.Ke4 Ke6 4.Kd4 Kf5.
step.capablancaMove.done:
Opposition regained: after 1...Kf8, 2.Kd3 waited off the file; when the black king came back to e7, 3.Ke3 restored three squares between the kings, with Black to move. 2.Kf2 also wins, because it leaves five squares between the kings on the f-file and Black to move; 2.Kf3?, however, would leave only four, and 2...Kf7 would draw. Had Black stayed on the e-file, the answer from the example would apply: 1.Ke2 Ke7 2.Ke3!

The main line is 1.Ke2 Kf8 2.Kd3 Ke7 3.Ke3.
2.Kf2 also works.
part.edge.title: Lateral approach
part.edge.summary: The squares controlled by the pawns show how to follow the opposing king.
step.t_edge: The target is the c6-pawn. 1.Kd6 looks like the shortest way. Is it?
step.t_edge.hint1: After 1.Kd6, where does the black king stand, and whose move is it?
step.t_edge.hint2: The kings are on the fifth rank; count the squares between them.
step.edge:
In the outflanking example the kings had room in the centre; now the edge restricts their routes. This training position comes from a study on distant opposition by Brandon2021.

1.Kd6? Kb6! and the kings stand on the same rank, with c6 between them and White to move: the white king does not get through, and it is a draw.

The right move is to step away: 1.Kf5! That leaves four squares between the kings, b5, c5, d5 and e5, and Black to move, but the black king cannot stay on the fifth rank, because b5 is covered by the c4-pawn. It has to go up, and the white king goes up with it, keeping three squares between them. Then the kings climb together on the same rank, and at the top the white king uses the edge to gain the move.
step.d_edge: Watch the kings climb on the same rank.
step.d_edge.m1: 1.Kf5! The white king steps away: the kings stand on a5 and f5, with four squares between them, and Black to move. The black king cannot answer on b5, which the c4-pawn covers.
step.d_edge.m2: 1...Kb6. The black king has to leave the fifth rank: b5 and b4 are covered by the c4- and a3-pawns. He goes up. Here is a common trap: the natural 2.Ke5? brings the king closer, but after 2...Kb7! Black draws; if the white king goes on to d6, 3...Kb6 puts the kings face to face on the sixth rank with White to move. What wins is 2.Kf6: the white king goes up as well and keeps the opposition along the rank.
step.d_edge.m3: 2.Kf6. The white king goes up with it: the kings stand on b6 and f6, with three squares between them, and Black to move. The c6-pawn stands on one of those squares, but the count is the same.
step.d_edge.m4: 2...Kb7. The black king goes up to b7, and the white king goes up with it to keep three squares between them on the same rank.
step.d_edge.m5: 3.Kf7. The kings are on the seventh rank, with three squares between them, and Black is still the one to move.
step.edgeMove: Play White and find the best move. The target is still the c6-pawn.
step.edgeMove.hint:
The shortest route to the pawn may surrender the opposition. Observe the squares your pawns deny the opposing king and look for a way to keep a route in from the side.

These do not work either:

At move 1
The closeness of c6 is misleading: access depends on opposition and the squares denied by the pawns.
If White played 1.Kd6?, Black would reply 1...Kb6 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.Kd6 Kb6 2.Ke5 Ka7.
If White played 1.Ke4?, Black would reply 1...Ka6 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.Ke4 Ka6 2.Kd3 Ka5.

At move 2
After the black king goes to a6, the route in must be kept along the sixth rank. Returning to the fifth or fourth gives the defender time to reorganise the opposition.
If White played 2.Ke4?, Black would reply 2...Kb6 and hold the draw. The line would be 2.Ke4 Kb6 3.Kd3 Ka5.
If White played 2.Ke5?, Black would reply 2...Ka7 and hold the draw. The line would be 2.Ke5 Ka7 3.Ke4 Ka6.
If White played 2.Kg5?, Black would reply 2...Ka7 and hold the draw. The line would be 2.Kg5 Ka7 3.Kf4 Ka6.

At move 3
Going forward without counting the turn gives away lateral opposition; approaching along the rank preserves access.
If White played 3.Kd7?, Black would reply 3...Kb7 and hold the draw. The line would be 3.Kd7 Kb7 4.Kd6 Kb6.
step.edgeMove.done:
Entry preserved: lateral opposition kept access to c6. Distance from the target matters less than the key squares available after the opponent’s reply.

The main line is 1.Kf5 Ka6 2.Ke6 Kb6 3.Kd6.
2.Kg6 also works.
3.Kf6 also works.
part.reserve.title: Spare tempo
part.reserve.summary: A free pawn move passes the turn and hands the opposition to the other side.
step.t_reserve: The black king has already reached e7, with five squares between the kings, and White is to move. The a2-pawn can still advance: that move is a reserve, able to change the turn without moving the king. How should that reserve be used?
step.t_reserve.hint1: Who has a move that changes nothing between the kings?
step.t_reserve.hint2: A pawn move passes the turn, and the turn decides the opposition.
step.reserve:
So far we have seen how to move the king to gain space or stop the opponent from getting in. A pawn that can still move adds another resource: the reserve, a move that changes the turn without moving the kings.

In this position the king also wins: 1.Ke2, for example, wins as well. The line uses 1.a3 to show the reserve: the white king is still on e1, the black one on e7, but now Black is to move. After 1...Ke6 2.Ke2 Ke5 3.Ke3, the white king shortens the distance and keeps the direct opposition.

The reserve is worth keeping because, in other positions, the king has no move that changes the turn without losing the opposition; the pawn does. But advancing a pawn also changes the structure, so changing the turn must serve the plan.
step.d_reserve: Watch the spare tempo hand the opposition over.
step.d_reserve.m1: 1.a3. The pawn passes the move without moving the kings. Black is to move with five squares between them.
step.d_reserve.m2: 1...Ke6. The black king advances, aiming to shorten the distance and keep the opposition. Now there are four squares between the kings, and White is to move. If White left the file with 2.Kd2?, Black would reply 2...Kd6! and have the opposition again, with three squares between the kings and White to move: a draw.
step.d_reserve.m3: 2.Ke2! The king shortens the distance and leaves three squares between the kings, with Black to move. It is the only winning move.
step.d_reserve.m4: 2...Ke5. The black king advances again; there are two squares between the kings, and White is to move. The natural 3.Kd3? would fail: 3...Kd5! would hand the direct opposition back to Black, with White to move.
step.d_reserve.m5: 3.Ke3. White takes direct opposition. The black king must give way, allowing the outflanking maneuver studied in Capablanca’s example.
step.grigorievMove: Play White and find the best move. The b2- and c3-pawns can still advance, and the white king is already close.
step.grigorievMove.hint:
Count the advances each side can use to pass the move. Bringing the king closer too early can remove every opposing square and cause stalemate; advancing a pawn too early can allow an exchange. Seek a waiting move that preserves your reserves and forces the opponent to spend theirs.

These do not work either:

At move 1
The order begins with the pawn structure: moving the king first, or spending both advances, lets Black draw.
If White played 1.Kb8?, Black would reply 1...b4 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.Kb8 b4 2.cxb4 Kb5.
If White played 1.b4?, Black would reply 1...Ka6 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.b4 Ka6 2.Kb8 Kb6.

At move 2
Waiting with the king preserves both the pawn reserve and the opponent’s escape squares. Approaching too early can cause stalemate; advancing a pawn too early spends the reserve or allows a capture.
If White played 2.Ka7?, Black would reply 2...b4 and hold the draw. The line would be 2.Ka7 b4 3.c4.
If White played 2.Kb7?, Black would reply 2...b4 and hold the draw. The line would be 2.Kb7 b4 3.c4.
If White played 2.b4+?, Black would reply 2...Ka6 and hold the draw. The line would be 2.b4+ Ka6 3.Kb8 Kb6.
If White played 2.c4?, Black would reply 2...bxc4 and hold the draw. The line would be 2.c4 bxc4 3.bxc4 Ka4.

At move 3
Capturing simplifies away the advantage; advancing without capturing keeps both pawns and passes the move.
If White played 3.cxb4+?, Black would reply 3...Kxb4 and hold the draw. The line would be 3.cxb4+ Kxb4 4.Ka7 Kxb3.
step.grigorievMove.done:
Patience rewarded: the waiting move preserves your reserves and the opposing squares needed to avoid stalemate. Only after the opponent spends their own tempo is it appropriate to change the structure.

The main line is 1.b3 Ka5 2.Kb8 b4 3.c4.
part.means.title: Choose the target
part.means.summary: The opposition is there to reach the key square or the pawn. If you can get there without it, do.
step.t_means: The white pawn is on c4. The lesson has shown ways to fight for opposition; now compare that technique with the aim of reaching a key square. Which move actually improves the route to promotion?
step.t_means.hint1: Where are the key squares of the c4-pawn? Can you reach them without going through the opposition?
step.means: First the target, then the technique. In this position 1.Ke4 takes the opposition and only draws after 1...Kd6. The advance 1.Kc5 wins because it brings the king closer to the key squares b6, c6 and d6. In the line, 1...Kd7 allows 2.Kb6, reaching one of them. Having the opposition is not a goal in itself: to win, it must help to promote or capture; to defend, it must stop the entry or allow counterplay.
step.d_means: Watch the white king go straight to the key square.
step.d_means.m1: 1.Kc5! No opposition at all: the king goes close to the key squares, with b6 and d6 within reach.
step.d_means.m2: 1...Kd7. The black king tries to block from the d-side.
step.d_means.m3: 2.Kb6. A key square of the c4-pawn. From here the pawn queens.
step.d_means.m4: 2...Kc8. He goes in front of the pawn.
step.d_means.m5: 3.Kc6. The white king controls b7, c7 and d7; so the black king only has the eighth rank.
step.d_means.m6: 3...Kb8. The black king only had b8 and d8. It went to b8, and now c8 is within the white king’s reach.
step.d_means.m7: 4.Kd7. The white king controls c8, and the pawn advances on its own to promotion.
step.recap:
Take three questions into your games.

1. What is the objective? Identify the key square, the pawn to protect or capture, and the entry the opponent threatens. Count the squares between the kings after making that choice.

2. What can change the turn? Check both sides’ reserves and the squares controlled by the pawns. Saving, spending or removing a reserve has different consequences; check the opponent’s reply before advancing.

3. Which relationship between the kings will be useful after the reply? Sometimes you must reach another rank, wait or outflank. A retreat can prepare entry or defence; moving closer helps only if it improves access to the objective.

In the exercises, apply these criteria to the actual position. The order of king and pawn moves depends on the advance’s purpose, the available route and the opposing threat.
step.finish: Play White and find the best move. The kings are on b2 and c7, and the f2-pawn is far from them: play until you queen.
ex.e09: Play White and find the best move. Your king starts in the corner, far from the d2-pawn. Find the first two king moves against the reply shown, preparing the approach through opposition.
ex.e09.hint:
First the black king's file, from afar. Then, every time he moves, shorten the distance facing him.

These do not work either:

At move 1
The king is still in the corner: advancing the pawn before bringing the king out lets the defender occupy the centre.
If White played 1.d3?, Black would reply 1...Kf7 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.d3 Kf7 2.d4 Ke6.
If White played 1.d4?, Black would reply 1...Kf7 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.d4 Kf7 2.d5 Kf6.

At move 2
The approach must shorten the distance; staying back on the second rank lets the black king establish its defence.
If White played 2.Kf2?, Black would reply 2...Ke6 and hold the draw. The line would be 2.Kf2 Ke6 3.d3 Kd5.

1.Kg2! takes distant opposition on the g-file, with five squares between the kings. After 1...Kf7, 2.Kf3! maintains opposition on the f-file, now with three intervening squares. The exercise ends here: you have prepared the approach and preserved the win, but a game would still require conversion.

If Black played 4...Ke4?, White would reply 5.Kc4 and win. The line would be 4...Ke4 5.Kc4 Ke5 6.Kc5.

With the black king on b4, you want yours on b2 with Black to move. Going to b2 at once gives Black the chance to answer with the pawn. Stay one step away from b2.

At move 1

If White played 1.Kb2?, Black would reply 1...d4 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.Kb2 d4 2.c3+ dxc3+.
If White played 1.c3+?, Black would reply 1...Kxc3 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.c3+ Kxc3 2.b4 Kxb4.

At move 2

If White played 2.Ka2?, Black would reply 2...Kxc2 and win. The line would be 2.Ka2 Kxc2 3.Ka3 d4.

At move 3

If White played 3.Kb2?, Black would reply 3...d4 and hold the draw. The line would be 3.Kb2 d4 4.c3+ dxc3+.

The b3-pawn must be preserved as a future promotion candidate. Advancing it allows a capture; in the continuation below, the final capture on c3 is en passant, immediately after White’s two-square pawn advance.
If White played 5.b4?, Black would reply 5...Kxb4 and hold the draw. The line would be 5.b4 Kxb4 6.c4 dxc3.

ex.e15: Play White and find the best move. In this 1932 study by {{Nikolai Grigoriev|nikolai-grigoriev}}, the black king threatens to return to the queenside and capture your pawns. Coordinate the white king’s route with the available pawn advances until you obtain a useful entry.
ex.e15.hint:
Identify each king’s target, the squares that restrict their routes and the pawn advances still available. Following the opposing king helps only if it preserves your pawns and prepares an entry. Save the reserve until changing the turn improves that struggle.

These do not work either:

At move 1
The king must improve its position before the pawns move: spending a reserve early lets the black king approach along a route sufficient to draw.
If White played 1.b3?, Black would reply 1...Ke1 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.b3 Ke1 2.c3 Kd2.
If White played 1.c3?, Black would reply 1...Kf3 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.c3 Kf3 2.b3 Ke3.
If White played 1.c4?, Black would reply 1...Ke1 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.c4 Ke1 2.b3 Kd1.

At move 2
Now is the time to move the c2-pawn away from the opposing king while keeping its second step. Delaying this decision allows an effective king entry or pawn advance by Black.
If White played 2.Kf5?, Black would reply 2...Kd2 and hold the draw. The line would be 2.Kf5 Kd2 3.c3 Kc2.
If White played 2.Kg3?, Black would reply 2...c4 and hold the draw. The line would be 2.Kg3 c4 3.b3 cxb3.

At move 3
The king must follow upwards; changing the queenside structure or retreating loses control of when to use the reserve.
If White played 3.b3?, Black would reply 3...Kd3 and hold the draw. The line would be 3.b3 Kd3 4.b4 cxb4.
If White played 3.b4?, Black would reply 3...cxb4 and hold the draw. The line would be 3.b4 cxb4 4.cxb4 Kd4.
If White played 3.Kg3?, Black would reply 3...c4 and win. The line would be 3.Kg3 c4 4.Kf2 Kd3.

At move 4
The reserve still needs to be kept. Advancing the supporting pawn can allow exchanges that eliminate the advantage.
If White played 4.b3?, Black would reply 4...c4 and hold the draw. The line would be 4.b3 c4 5.bxc4 Kd6.
If White played 4.b4?, Black would reply 4...cxb4 and hold the draw. The line would be 4.b4 cxb4 5.cxb4 Kd4.

At move 5
Spending an advance before reaching the right position gives the black king time to return to the queenside.
If White played 5.b3?, Black would reply 5...c4 and hold the draw. The line would be 5.b3 c4 6.bxc4 Ke5.
If White played 5.c4?, Black would reply 5...Ke5 and hold the draw. The line would be 5.c4 Ke5 6.b3 Kd4.

Moving one square higher does not solve the turn problem: the pawn reserve or the winning retreat must be assessed from the actual position.
If White played 6.Kg8?, Black would reply 6...Kf6 and hold the draw. The line would be 6.Kg8 Kf6 7.b3 c4.

At move 7
After spending the reserve, the outflanking opportunity must be used; returning to the previous plan can give back the draw.
If White played 7.b3?, Black would reply 7...Ke7 and hold the draw. The line would be 7.b3 Ke7 8.Kg6 Ke6.
If White played 7.Kg6?, Black would reply 7...Ke5 and hold the draw. The line would be 7.Kg6 Ke5 8.b3 Kd4.

At move 8
The king must enter the square that keeps the advantage in the struggle for the targets, not merely approach along the eighth rank.
If White played 8.Ke8?, Black would reply 8...Kd4 and hold the draw. The line would be 8.Ke8 Kd4 9.Kd7 Kxc4.

1.Kg4!, and after 1...Ke3, 2.c3! The pawn leaves the black king's reach and keeps its second step, c4, for later. The kings climb on the same rank, 3.Kg5 Ke5, 4.Kg6 Ke6, 5.Kg7 Ke7, with one square between them and White to move: the opposition along the rank is Black's. On the seventh rank, 6.c4! uses the reserve to change the turn without moving the kings. The retreat 6.Kg6 also preserves the win, whereas after 6.Kg8? Black draws by replying 6...Kf6. Being near the edge requires choosing the square and the turn carefully, rather than simply continuing upwards. After 6...Ke6, 7.Kf8! and 8.Ke7 go round the black king and reach the c5-pawn first. On the first move, 1.c3 allows 1...Kf3 with the opposition for Black; on the second, 2.c4 lets the black king come back.

At move 2
The h7 target must be fixed before the approach continues. If the king moves, Black can prevent the same plan with a pawn advance or gain time on the queenside.
If White played 2.Ke3?, Black would reply 2...Kc6 and win. The line would be 2.Ke3 Kc6 3.Kd4 Kb5.
If White played 2.Kf3?, Black would reply 2...h6 and win. The line would be 2.Kf3 h6 3.Ke3 Kc6.
If White played 2.Kg3?, Black would reply 2...h6 and win. The line would be 2.Kg3 h6 3.Kf3 Kc6.

At move 3
If White played 3.Ke3? or 3.Kf3?, Black would reply 3...Kd5 and win: after 4.Kf4 Kd4, the kings stand on f4 and d4, on the same rank, with e4 between them and White to move. The lateral opposition belongs to Black: the black king controls e4, and the white king cannot cross that square.

At move 4
If White played 4.Kf4? or 4.Kg4?, Black would also win: 4.Kf4 Kd4 5.Kg4 Ke4 and 4.Kg4 Ke4 5.Kh4 Kf4 end with the kings on the same rank, one square between them and White to move. Reaching the fourth rank was not enough: in that confrontation it is the white king that has to give way, and the counterplay against h7 does not arrive.

At move 5
Entering g5 too early lets the black king capture e5 and then reach f6, blocking the route to the target.
If White played 5.Kg5?, Black would reply 5...Kxe5 and win. The line would be 5.Kg5 Kxe5 6.Kg4 Kf6.

At move 6
The timing of the entry matters: occupying g5 before Black’s capture does not produce the same opposition as occupying it afterwards.
If White played 6.Kg5?, Black would reply 6...Kxe5 and win. The line would be 6.Kg5 Kxe5 7.Kg4 Kf6.

At move 7
After e5 is captured, retreating abandons the counterplay; pressure on the fixed target must be maintained.
If White played 7.Kf3?, Black would reply 7...Kd4 and win. The line would be 7.Kf3 Kd4 8.Ke2 Ke4.
ex.e16.solution:
1.Kf2!! 1.Ke2? takes the opposition and loses: 1...Kd7!, 2...Kc6, 3...Kb5, and the black king goes round. 1.h6? loses to 1...Kf7. The white king's target is the h7-pawn: after 1...Kd7, 2.h6! fixes it, and the king heads for the kingside, always in step with the black king: 2...Kc6 3.Kg3!, 3...Kd5 4.Kh4!, 4...Kd4 5.Kh5!, 5...Ke4 6.Kg4!, 6...Kxe5 7.Kg5! In the last two moves the kings stand on the same rank, on the same rank, with one square between them and Black to move: the black king gives way, and the white one reaches f6 and the h7-pawn. If 1...Ke7, 2.Kf3!!, for the same reason. Every white move in the line is the only one that draws.

These do not work either:

At move 1: Opposition in the centre does not protect the decisive objective. The white king must prepare kingside counterplay before the black king outflanks. If White played 1.Kd2?, Black would reply 1...Kd7 and win. The line would be 1.Kd2 Kd7 2.Kc3 Kc6. If White played 1.Ke2?, Black would reply 1...Kd7 and win. The line would be 1.Ke2 Kd7 2.Kd3 Kc6.

At move 2: The h7 target must be fixed before the approach continues. If the king moves, Black can prevent the same plan with a pawn advance or gain time on the queenside. If White played 2.Ke3?, Black would reply 2...Kc6 and win. The line would be 2.Ke3 Kc6 3.Kd4 Kb5. If White played 2.Kf3?, Black would reply 2...h6 and win. The line would be 2.Kf3 h6 3.Ke3 Kc6. If White played 2.Kg3?, Black would reply 2...h6 and win. The line would be 2.Kg3 h6 3.Kf3 Kc6.

At move 3: If White played 3.Ke3? or 3.Kf3?, Black would reply 3...Kd5 and win: after 4.Kf4 Kd4, the kings stand on f4 and d4, on the same rank, with e4 between them and White to move. The lateral opposition belongs to Black: the black king controls e4, and the white king cannot cross that square.

At move 4: If White played 4.Kf4? or 4.Kg4?, Black would also win: 4.Kf4 Kd4 5.Kg4 Ke4 and 4.Kg4 Ke4 5.Kh4 Kf4 end with the kings on the same rank, one square between them and White to move. Reaching the fourth rank was not enough: in that confrontation it is the white king that has to give way, and the counterplay against h7 does not arrive.
