At move 6: The timing of the entry matters: occupying g5 before Black’s capture does not produce the same opposition as occupying it afterwards. If White played 6.Kg5?, Black would reply 6...Kxe5 and win. The line would be 6.Kg5 Kxe5 7.Kg4 Kf6.

At move 7: After e5 is captured, retreating abandons the counterplay; pressure on the fixed target must be maintained. If White played 7.Kf3?, Black would reply 7...Kd4 and win. The line would be 7.Kf3 Kd4 8.Ke2 Ke4.
key.lesson: The white king takes the opposition from far away, with several squares between the kings, and closes the gap step by step until it reaches the deciding squares in front of the pawn.
key.diagonal: The opposition works along the diagonal too: the white king stands on the same diagonal as the black king and, step by step, turns it into face-to-face opposition.
key.means: The opposition is a means, not the goal: here taking it only draws. What wins is taking the king straight to the deciding squares in front of the pawn.
key.capablanca: {{Capablanca|jose-raul-capablanca}}'s example: locked pawns on both sides and the kings far apart. Whoever is to move takes the distant opposition and wins.
key.carlsenSo: {{Magnus Carlsen|magnus-carlsen}}, playing White, faced {{Wesley So|wesley-so}}, playing Black, at {{Norway Chess|norway-chess}} in {{Stavanger|stavanger}} in 2017. Black was a pawn down and needed to prevent the white king from entering. The black king retreated to obtain distant opposition and followed its opponent from file to file; the game ended in a draw.
key.euweWhitaker: {{Max Euwe|max-euwe}}, playing White, faced {{Norman Whitaker|norman-whitaker}}, playing Black, in The Hague in 1928. The white king obtained distant opposition on the same rank as the black king, approaching the opposing pawn without allowing an equivalent race on the other wing. White won; observe how the kings’ relative positions help reach the target.
history:
Opposition is the contest between kings to force the opponent to give up space; it can begin at a distance or along a diagonal. The goal is to reach an important square, capture a pawn, or prevent an opposing entry. In his 1921 book Chess Fundamentals, {{José Raúl Capablanca|jose-raul-capablanca}} explains the topic as an author through pawn-ending examples.

The technique also appears in games: at {{Norway Chess|norway-chess}} in {{Stavanger|stavanger}} in 2017, {{Wesley So|wesley-so}}, playing Black, defended an ending a pawn down against {{Magnus Carlsen|magnus-carlsen}}, playing White. The black king followed the white king from a distance, and the game ended in a draw. Just a few pieces can conceal a precise contest for space and time.
practice: Now the real ending: king on h3, pawn on f3, and the black king on e6, in front of the key squares. Find the diagonal, turn it into direct opposition and queen the pawn. Pick your pace and go.
step.d_outflank.m1: 4.Kf4. The king follows on the f-file and controls g4 and g5. This keeps the route to the h4-pawn closed.
step.d_outflank.m2: 4...Kg6. The black king leaves the f-file to remain close to the h5-pawn. The route through the center is now open.
step.d_outflank.m3: 5.Ke5. Now going round has a safe goal: approach Black’s b5-pawn through the centre while the black king is far away. White’s b4-pawn is covered on the way, and the earlier preparation prevented an equivalent race against h4.
part.outflank.title: Outflanking
part.outflank.summary: Before going around the other side, prevent the opposing king from reaching your pawns.
step.t_outflank: Direct opposition has already been reached, and the black king has stepped away to f6. Black’s b5-pawn looks close, but White’s h4-pawn also needs protecting. Should the king go round at once or follow once more?
step.t_outflank.hint1: Compare your king’s route to b5 with the opposing king’s route to h4.
step.t_outflank.hint2: Before changing wings, look for a way to deny the black king squares on its approach.
step.outflank: Going round means passing along the wing the enemy king has left free. The passage is only useful if it does not hand over an equally important target. In this position 4.Kf4 keeps the opposition and covers the approach to h4. After 4...Kg6, 5.Ke5 switches the target to Black’s b5-pawn. The pawn structure decides when to follow and when to go round.
step.d_outflank: Watch first how the black king is restricted, then the entry through the centre.
step.outflankMove: Play White and find the best move. White’s h4-pawn also needs protecting.
step.outflankMove.hint:
Look at the target the opposing king could reach if you changed wings now.

These do not work either:

At move 4
Switching early to the queenside lets the black king advance toward h4. That counterplay must first be restricted.
If White played 4.Kd4?, Black would reply 4...Kf5 and hold the draw. The line would be 4.Kd4 Kf5 5.Kc5 Kg4.
If White played 4.Kd5?, Black would reply 4...Kf5 and hold the draw. The line would be 4.Kd5 Kf5 5.Kd4 Kf4.

At move 5
After restricting the kingside, more than one central route wins. Retreating to g3, however, lets Black regain activity.
If White played 5.Kg3?, Black would reply 5...Kf5 and hold the draw. The line would be 5.Kg3 Kf5 6.Kf3 Ke5.
step.outflankMove.done:
Going round at the right time: 4.Kf4 took g4 and g5 away from the black king, and only then did the white king enter through the centre with 5.Ke5. 5.Ke4 also wins: the h4-pawn covers g5, and the king covers f5.

The main line is 4.Kf4 Kg6 5.Ke5.
5.Ke4 also works.
step.d_edgeCorner.m1: 1.Ke8. Waiting prepares the return to the seventh rank after the defender’s reply.
step.d_edgeCorner.m2: 1...Ka7. The defender returns to the seventh rank. This is a common trap: the natural 2.Kd7? shortens the distance, but 2...Kb7! leaves the kings on b7 and d7, with one square between them and White to move; the opposition belongs to Black, and Black draws. What wins is 2.Ke7, with three squares between the kings and Black to move.
step.d_edgeCorner.m3: 2.Ke7. Three squares separate the kings and Black moves. This opposition prepares entry, but does not yet capture a pawn.
part.edgeCorner.title: At the edge
part.edgeCorner.summary: A waiting square makes it possible to regain the opposition without abandoning the target.
step.t_edgeCorner: The kings have already climbed the board. The white king is on f7 and wants to reach c6; the black king has returned to b6. Which waiting move lets White continue the struggle for opposition at the edge?
step.t_edgeCorner.hint1: The square nearest the target is not always the one that preserves the route in.
step.t_edgeCorner.hint2: Consider the rank still available behind your king and the opponent’s replies on the seventh.
step.edgeCorner:
The black king protects c6 and tries to answer the white king’s approaches along the same rank. Near the edge, the waiting move must produce a useful entry.

The line 1.Ke8 Ka7 2.Ke7 leaves three squares between the kings on the seventh rank, with Black to move. After 2...Kb7 the plan changes: it is time to use d7 as a passage, keeping Black on move.

With 3.Kd7! Kb6 4.Kd6, the black king has to leave b6. If it chooses 4...Ka5, 5.Kxc5 captures a pawn and keeps the white king protecting c4. Pressing c6 does not mean it will be the first pawn captured: after the capture, the safety of the white pawn counts too.

Compare 3.Kd6? Kb6! The same alignment on the sixth rank arises with White to move, and Black draws. The regained opposition must turn into an entry at the right moment.
step.d_edgeCorner: First White regains the opposition; then uses the d7 passage to force the black king to give way next to the pawns.
step.edgeCornerMove: Play White and find the best move. The white king is on f7; the black one, on b6, protects c6.
step.edgeCornerMove.hint: After waiting, compare who will move after your entry. The defender must not be able to answer on the same rank and pass the obligation to move back to you.
step.edgeCornerMove.done: In the main line, the wait 1.Ke8 regained the opposition on the seventh rank, and 3.Kd7 went through the useful passage, with Black to move. Opposition served to make the defender give way near c6 and c5; the capture depends on its chosen reply.
step.reserveMove: Play White and find the best move. The a2-pawn can still advance.
step.reserveMove.hint:
A reserve can change whose turn it is without moving the kings. Once it has served that purpose, another advance may allow capture by the b-pawn. Compare the opposition obtained by each king approach; stepping sideways may return the favorable turn to the opponent.

These do not work either:

At move 2
The reserve has already served its purpose. Another pawn advance allows capture by the b-pawn, while leaving the correct file lets the black king regain opposition. The king must now approach at the correct distance.
If White played 2.a4?, Black would reply 2...bxa4 and hold the draw. The line would be 2.a4 bxa4 3.Kd1 a3.
If White played 2.Kd2?, Black would reply 2...Kd6 and hold the draw. The line would be 2.Kd2 Kd6 3.a4 bxa4.
If White played 2.Kf2?, Black would reply 2...Kd5 and hold the draw. The line would be 2.Kf2 Kd5 3.Ke2 Kc4.

At move 3
On the final approach, a sideways deviation lets the black king follow. Preserving the win requires converting distant opposition into direct opposition without spending another reserve at the wrong time.
If White played 3.Kd3?, Black would reply 3...Kd5 and hold the draw. The line would be 3.Kd3 Kd5 4.a4 bxa4.
If White played 3.Kf3?, Black would reply 3...Kf5 and hold the draw. The line would be 3.Kf3 Kf5 4.Ke2 Ke4.
step.reserveMove.done:
The reserve at the right moment: 1.a3 passed the turn without moving the kings; then 2.Ke2 and 3.Ke3 turned the distant opposition into direct opposition. Here king moves also win; the line uses 1.a3 to show the reserve. 3.Ke1 also wins: it leaves three squares, e2, e3 and e4, between the kings, with Black to move.

The main line is 1.a3 Ke6 2.Ke2 Ke5 3.Ke3.
1.Kd1, 1.Kd2, 1.Ke2, 1.Kf1 and 1.Kf2 also work.
3.Ke1 also works.
step.d_waiting.m1: 1.b3. The advance preserves the two-pawn structure and prepares the waiting plan. Spending both steps at once would allow a draw.
step.d_waiting.m2: 1...Ka5. The black king moves to the edge and keeps its pawn advance available. This is a common trap: the natural 2.Kb7? brings the king right up, but after 2...b4! the move 3.c4 leaves the black king without moves, and it is stalemate; 3.cxb4+ Kxb4 also draws. What wins is 2.Kb8: the king waits a little further away and does not take the black king's squares too early.
step.d_waiting.m3: 2.Kb8. This is the king’s waiting move: it stays close without taking away the opponent’s squares too early. Approaching now can allow stalemate after the pawn advances.
step.d_waiting.m4: 2...b4. Black spends its reserve. Only now is it useful to employ the waiting move of White’s other pawn.
step.d_waiting.m5: 3.c4. The pawn passes the move without capturing. The win remains, and the black king still has squares: the reserve worked because the king’s approach was delayed.
part.waiting.title: Waiting with kings
part.waiting.summary: Before using the pawn reserve, it may be necessary to wait with the king.
step.t_waiting: In this study attributed to {{Nikolai Grigoriev|nikolai-grigoriev}}, from 1930, White has two pawns against one. The king is already close, but bringing it closer too quickly may help the defence. How should the king’s and pawns’ waiting moves be coordinated?
step.t_waiting.hint1: Compare how many advances each side can still make without moving its king.
step.t_waiting.hint2: A king that comes too close can also take away every square from an opponent that is not in check. Keep a waiting move before bringing it closer.
step.waiting: In the reserve part, a pawn changed the turn without moving the kings; at the edge, we saw a waiting move prepare opposition. Now those resources must be combined. After 1.b3 Ka5, 2.Kb8 waits with the king. If it approaches with 2.Ka7? b4 3.c4, Black has no legal move and is not in check: that is stalemate, and therefore a draw. In the winning line, 2...b4 3.c4 passes the move while the white king is still farther away. Here, waiting avoids stalemate; in other positions, it may keep pawns protected or prepare opposition after the opponent spends a reserve. The test is what the waiting move preserves and which reply it allows.
step.d_waiting: Observe three stages: prepare the pawn structure, wait with the king, and only then pass the move with the other pawn.
step.meansMove: Play White and find the best move. The key squares of the c4-pawn are b6, c6 and d6.
step.meansMove.hint:
Compare a square that merely faces the other king with one that brings you closer to the goal. If the pawn advances without support, the opposing king can catch it; prepare its promotion before pushing it.

These do not work either:

At move 1
Advancing the pawn before the king allows it to be caught and captured. The key square serves the concrete goal of supporting promotion.
If White played 1.c5?, Black would reply 1...Kd7 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.c5 Kd7 2.c6+ Kxc6.
step.meansMove.done:
1.Kc5! went straight for the key squares, without fighting for the opposition. In the line, 2.Kb6 reaches a key square to support promotion. The alternatives 2.Kb5 and 2.Kd5 also preserve the win, but do not reach a key square on that move: each requires its own continuation.

The main line is 1.Kc5 Kd7 2.Kb6.
2.Kb5 and 2.Kd5 also work.
part.fixedTarget.title: Fix first
part.fixedTarget.summary: Fix the distant pawn before organizing the king’s defensive route.
step.t_fixedTarget: In this 1920 study by Grigoriev, the black king threatens to capture h3 and support its passed pawn. On the other wing, Black’s a5-pawn can still advance. What is the first move?
step.t_fixedTarget.hint1: Before starting the king’s race, examine the pawn moves Black can still keep in reserve.
step.t_fixedTarget.hint2: A blocked pawn loses its freedom to advance. That difference in timing matters when the kings must face each other.
step.fixedTarget: So far, pawn advances have saved or spent reserves and freed a pawn after its blocker was captured. An advance can also fix an opposing pawn: block it so that it cannot advance. Here, 1.a4 is the only drawing move. It fixes the a5-pawn and removes a black reserve that could change the turn during the defence. After 1...Kg3 2.Ke6 Kxh3 3.Kf5, White has given up h3 but retained a defensive route. Fixing a pawn does not always mean attacking it: in this study, the purpose is to remove its mobility. In another structure, fixation may create a target; check the route to it and what the opponent threatens in the meantime.
step.d_fixedTarget: Observe the order: first block the distant reserve, then bring the king to the defense.
step.fixedTargetMove: Play White and find the best move. The black king threatens to capture h3, and the a5-pawn can still advance.
step.fixedTargetMove.hint:
An immediate king race leaves the opponent a resource on the other wing. Remove that resource before bringing the king closer.

These do not work either:

At move 1
Fixation comes before the race: without it, Black retains the distant reserve and can combine play on both sides of the board.
If White played 1.Kc6?, Black would reply 1...Kg3 and win. The line would be 1.Kc6 Kg3 2.Kb5 Kxh3.
If White played 1.Kd6?, Black would reply 1...Kg3 and win. The line would be 1.Kd6 Kg3 2.Ke5 Kxh3.
If White played 1.Ke6?, Black would reply 1...a4 and win. The line would be 1.Ke6 a4 2.Kd5 h5.

At move 2
After fixation, diverting the king to the queenside or advancing h3 leaves the black king an effective route to support the passed pawn. The defense requires reaching the kingside in time.
If White played 2.Kc6?, Black would reply 2...Kxh3 and win. The line would be 2.Kc6 Kxh3 3.Kb5 h5.
If White played 2.h4?, Black would reply 2...Kxh4 and win. The line would be 2.h4 Kxh4 3.Kc6 h5.

At move 3
The king must reach a square from which it can coordinate with the next advance. The deviations to d5 or f6 do not prepare that coordination and lose.
If White played 3.Kd5?, Black would reply 3...h5 and win. The line would be 3.Kd5 h5 4.Ke4 Kg3.
If White played 3.Kf6?, Black would reply 3...h5 and win. The line would be 3.Kf6 h5 4.Ke5 h4.
step.fixedTargetMove.done:
Fixing at the right time: in this study, fixing the distant reserve prepares the defensive route. Losing h3 does not decide the result: the defense depends on coordinating the king with Black’s moves.

The main line is 1.a4 Kg3 2.Ke6 Kxh3 3.Kf5.
step.err_distantKing.m1: 1...Ke7. The black king occupies the same file, with three squares between the kings and White to move.
step.err_distantKing.m2: 2.g4. The pawn advance changes the turn but does not take the white king to a key square.
step.err_distantKing.m3: 2...Ke6. The black king shortens the distance and stands in front of the pawn. White can no longer reach a key square.
step.err_distantKing: The white king has come only as far as e3. Watch how the defence organises the opposition.
step.err_distantPawn.m1: 1...Kd7. The black king approaches through the centre while the white king remains behind the pawn.
step.err_distantPawn.m2: 2.g5. The next advance gains ground for the pawn but does not solve its king’s insufficient position.
step.err_distantPawn.m3: 2...Kd6. The black king reaches the centre in time to defend, and White can no longer reach a key square.
step.err_distantPawn: The white pawn advanced before its king gained space. Observe the defender’s central route.
step.err_diagonalKing.m1: 1...Ke6. Black faces the opposing king, with one square between them and White to move.
step.err_diagonalKing.m2: 2.Kd3. The white king must look for another route; the direct approach did not secure a way through.
step.err_diagonalKing.m3: 2...Kd5. The defence follows onto the new file and keeps direct opposition. The position is drawn.
step.err_diagonalKing: The white king chose the direct entry on e4. Follow the opposition obtained by Black.
step.err_diagonalCheck.m1: 1...Ke6. The king escapes the check and continues preventing entry in front of the pawn.
step.err_diagonalCheck.m2: 2.e5. The pawn advances again. The white king has still not established a winning position.
step.err_diagonalCheck.m3: 2...Kd7. The king retreats safely; the defence preserves the draw. The active-looking check did not compensate for missing the key square.
step.err_diagonalCheck: The white pawn has just given check, but the king did not occupy the available key square. See why the check is not decisive.
step.err_defendClose.m1: 1.Kf4. White takes direct opposition, with Black to move.
step.err_defendClose.m2: 1...Kg6. The black king gives way on the file. White already has a winning continuation.
step.err_defendClose.m3: 2.Kg4. The white king follows and maintains opposition, preparing to enter the key squares.
step.err_defendClose: Black brought the king closer too early. Now follow White, which can gain space.
step.err_defendRetreat.m1: 1.Kf5. The white king reaches a key square for the pawn and preserves the win.
step.err_defendRetreat.m2: 1...Kg7. The black king tries to stay in front, but has already conceded a decisive position.
step.err_defendRetreat.m3: 2.Kg5. The white king occupies another key square and keeps the winning position.
step.err_defendRetreat: Black retreated when it needed to guard the key squares. Watch the white king enter.
step.err_lateralFile.m1: 1.Kb5. The white king descends towards the important squares for supporting its pawn.
step.err_lateralFile.m2: 1...Ke6. Black tries to correct the route, but White already has time to advance.
step.err_lateralFile.m3: 2.Kc5. The white king gains ground. The defence arrived too late to maintain the lateral barrier.
step.err_lateralFile: The black king moved down without adjusting its file. Now follow the space gained by White.
step.err_lateralDistance.m1: 1.Kc4. The white king reaches a key square for the d2-pawn.
step.err_lateralDistance.m2: 1...Kc6. The black king tries to obtain opposition on the file, but the important entry has already happened.
step.err_lateralDistance.m3: 2.d3. The pawn advances with support from its king’s position. White’s advantage remains winning.
step.err_lateralDistance: The black king kept the wrong distance along the rank. Follow White’s entry.
step.err_capablanca.m1: 1...Ke7. Black returns to the e-file with three squares between the kings and White to move.
step.err_capablanca.m2: 2.Kd3. The white king changes direction, but can no longer force the same route through.
step.err_capablanca.m3: 2...Kf6. The defence can reorganise on the other wing. The position remains drawn despite the white king’s apparent initiative.
step.err_capablanca: The white king advanced straight ahead after the opposing king changed file. See who obtains the opposition.
step.err_edge.m1: 1...Kb6. The black king takes lateral opposition: one square between the kings, with White to move.
step.err_edge.m2: 2.Ke5. The white king turns back to look for another route. The earlier approach did not secure the capture.
step.err_edge.m3: 2...Ka7. The black king maintains a sufficient defence. Access to the pawn has not been won.
step.err_edge: The white king rushed directly to d6. The pawn looks close, but opposition determines access.
step.err_waitStalemate.m1: 1...b4. Black advances the pawn and prepares a position with no available king moves.
step.err_waitStalemate.m2: 2.c4. Black now has no legal move and is not in check: it is stalemate. The position is drawn immediately.
step.err_waitStalemate: The white king approached a7 before Black’s reserve was spent. Observe the stalemate resource.
step.err_waitCapture.m1:
1...Kxb4. Before choosing how to support a pawn, complete the recapture: which white pawn remains, what threat does it face and where is your king?

The b3-pawn remains, threatened by the black king on b4. The white king is on b8, too far away to defend it on the next move. Bringing the king closer will only help if the pawn survives first.
step.err_waitCapture.m2: 2.Ka7. Bringing the king closer does not solve the immediate threat to b3: from a7, it still cannot reach the defence of that pawn on this move.
step.err_waitCapture.m3: 2...Kxb3 draws: only the kings remain. First check what survives the capture and recapture; only then plan how to support that pawn. Here the immediate threat eliminated the last candidate before the white king could reach it.
step.err_waitCapture: White captured instead of waiting and gave up the win. Before each move, count the remaining pawns and check whether the white king can protect the survivor.
part.secondReserve.title: Save a tempo
part.secondReserve.summary: Keep the second advance for when the king’s route needs a change of turn.
step.t_secondReserve: The black king is close to the queenside pawns, and White’s c2-pawn can still advance one or two squares. There are also pawns on the h-file, which change the kings’ routes. How can White advance without spending a reserve that may be needed later?
step.t_secondReserve.hint1: Two one-square advances change the turn twice; one double advance does so only once.
step.t_secondReserve.hint2: Besides the distance between the kings, observe the sixth-rank square controlled by Black’s h7-pawn.
step.secondReserve:
The white king is on g4; the black king, on e3.

A pawn on the second rank can give two separate tempi if it advances one square at a time. Spending both steps at once changes the structure and removes the second waiting move.

The line 1.c3 Ke4 2.Kg5 Ke5 keeps the pawn’s advance to c4 in hand. Now h7 controls g6 and stops the white king from climbing through that square: it is this obstacle that decides when to use the reserve.

In that position 3.c4 changes the turn while the white king stays close to the h7-pawn. 3.h6?, however, draws: Black replies with the advance of the c5-pawn, in the centre. Not every pawn advance is an equivalent waiting move; one of them can block the king’s own route.

With the pawn on c4, the reserve has been used. In the continuation 3...Kd4, the black king approaches c4 but moves away from h7. The next part starts from that structure: the new plan is to enter via h6, capture h7 and free the h-pawn before Black’s counterplay arrives.
step.d_secondReserve: The second advance is kept until it is needed; once it is spent, White watches Black’s reply and uses the entry it allows.
step.d_secondReserve.m1: 1.c3. The pawn leaves c2 without spending the second advance to c4. White keeps a tempo to change the turn later, while the king prepares access to Black’s h7-pawn.
step.d_secondReserve.m2: 1...Ke4. The black king advances and tries to keep facing its opponent along the rank.
step.d_secondReserve.m3: 2.Kg5. The white king follows upwards and keeps the win. The c3-pawn remains available as a reserve.
step.d_secondReserve.m4: 2...Ke5. The kings stand on the same rank with one square between them and White to move. Progress up the g-file is restricted by the h7-pawn.
step.d_secondReserve.m5: 3.c4. The reserve changes the turn at the useful moment. The black king must choose a reply, and White preserves a winning route to the h7 target.
step.secondReserveMove: Play White and find the best move. The c2-pawn can still advance one or two squares.
step.secondReserveMove.hint:
Compare what changes when a pawn advances one or two squares. Before moving the king up, check the squares controlled by pawns. Fixing the target too early may also allow an opposing central advance: spend the reserve when it improves the position.

These do not work either:

At move 3
Fixing h7 with the pawn now allows 3...c4: Black’s central resource changes the structure before the target is captured.
If White played 3.h6?, Black would reply 3...c4 and hold the draw. The line would be 3.h6 c4 4.Kg4 Ke4.
step.secondReserveMove.done:
Second reserve kept: the c-pawn advanced one square at a time, and the second step was only spent when changing the turn improved the position. The reserve and the squares controlled by the h7-pawn determine the order of actions.

The main line is 1.c3 Ke4 2.Kg5 Ke5 3.c4.
1.Kf5 and 1.Kg5 also work.
2.b3, 2.b4 and 2.Kh4 also work.
3.b3, 3.b4, 3.Kg4, 3.Kh4 and 3.Kh6 also work.
step.d_useReserve: After using the reserve, White turns the change in the position into a concrete target.
step.d_useReserve.m1: 4.Kh6. The white king approaches h7 through h6, avoiding g6, which the black pawn controls.
step.d_useReserve.m2: 4...Kd3. The black king continues its plan to capture on the other wing. White retains the advantage in the race between the targets.
step.d_useReserve.m3: 5.Kxh7. The h7 target is captured. White’s h-pawn can advance.
step.d_useReserve.m4: 5...Kxc4. Black also captures a pawn, but this reply does not eliminate White’s win.
step.d_useReserve.m5: 6.h6. Now the pawn advance serves promotion. Earlier, the correct reserve had to be preserved; after capturing the blocker, the objective has changed.
step.d_useReserve.m6: 6...Kb3. The black king continues on the queenside. White retains a winning position with the h-pawn free.
step.err_reserve_early_c4: White spent both advances of the c2-pawn at once. Observe Black’s approach to the base of the pawns.
step.err_reserve_early_c4.m1: 1...Kd3. The black king changes direction and approaches the queenside pawns.
step.err_reserve_early_c4.m2: 2.b3. The advance tries to reorganise the structure, but the c-pawn’s reserve has already been spent.
step.err_reserve_early_c4.m3: 2...Kc2. The black king approaches the base of the pawns and retains enough resources to draw.
step.err_reserve_early_c4.m4: 3.b4. The pawn advances, but the position remains drawn. The space gained by the double advance did not replace the tempo that was lost.
step.err_reserve_early_h6: In this position, White advanced the h-pawn instead of using the c-file reserve. Observe Black’s central resource.
step.err_reserve_early_h6.m1: 1...c4. Black advances its own pawn. The blockade changes the queenside struggle before the white king can capture h7.
step.err_reserve_early_h6.m2: 2.Kg4. The white king turns back, but no longer has the same winning continuation.
step.err_reserve_early_h6.m3: 2...Ke4. The black king approaches and preserves equality. Fixing h7 now did not compensate for the central resource.
step.err_reserve_early_h6.m4: 3.Kg3. The white king tries to reorganise. The position remains drawn: a reserve useful in another position can be premature here.
part.useReserve.title: Use the reserve
part.useReserve.summary: After changing the turn, choose the target and route that preserve the win.
step.t_useReserve: The reserve has been used, and the black king has moved down to d4. The white king needs to turn this change into a concrete threat. Which route reaches the h7-pawn without crossing a square it controls?
step.t_useReserve.hint1: A pawn controls the diagonals in front of it, not the square immediately ahead.
step.t_useReserve.hint2: Compare the route along the g-file with approaching on the pawn’s own file.
step.useReserve: The reserve fulfilled its purpose because it created a useful continuation. Here, 4.Kh6 approaches the blocker from the front, avoiding g6, which the h7-pawn controls. After 4...Kd3, 5.Kxh7 removes the blocker. Even after 5...Kxc4, 6.h6 preserves the win. The pawn advance now serves promotion; earlier, it served to manage the turn.
step.useReserveMove: Play White and find the best move. The h7-pawn controls g6.
step.useReserveMove.hint:
Check pawn control before choosing the king’s route. Advancing your own pawn before capturing the blocker may give time for captures on the other wing. Once the blocker is gone, reconsider whether keeping the advance in reserve is still necessary.

These do not work either:

At move 4
The king’s route and the pawn advance are not interchangeable. Fixing h7 early allows captures on the queenside; the king’s approach preserves the win. Another tempo with the b-pawn is also sufficient.
If White played 4.h6?, Black would reply 4...Kxc4 and hold the draw. The line would be 4.h6 Kxc4 5.b3+ Kxb3.
step.useReserveMove.done:
Conversion complete. The goal changed along the way: first capture the blocker, then promote. When to spend the reserve follows that plan.

The main line is 4.Kh6 Kd3 5.Kxh7 Kxc4 6.h6.
4.b3 also works.
5.b3 and 5.Kg7 also work.
6.Kg6, 6.Kg7, 6.Kg8, 6.Kh6 and 6.Kh8 also work.
step.d_fixedTarget.m1: 1.a4. The pawn on a5 is blocked. Fixation removes a resource Black could use to change whose turn it is.
step.d_fixedTarget.m2: 1...Kg3. The black king attacks h3. White needs a precise route rather than to preserve every pawn.
step.d_fixedTarget.m3: 2.Ke6. The king uses the diagonal to reach f5 in time.
step.d_fixedTarget.m4: 2...Kxh3. Black captures h3. The position remains drawn: the white king can organize the defense against the passed pawn.
step.d_fixedTarget.m5: 3.Kf5. The king reaches the defensive area. In the next part, we will see how to meet the h-pawn’s advance.
part.synchronize.title: Coordinate the defense
part.synchronize.summary: Fixation allows the king to follow along the appropriate rank and stop the passed pawn.
step.t_synchronize: Black has just advanced the pawn to h5. The a5-pawn is already fixed, and the defence depends on the kings’ timing. Which retreat of the white king prepares the barrier?
step.t_synchronize.hint1: Do not calculate only the distance to the pawn. Compare the ranks the kings can occupy after its next advance.
step.t_synchronize.hint2: Prepare a position where the kings face each other on the same rank, with the opponent to move.
step.synchronize:
The white king is on f5; the black king, on h3.

Now the defence is against the passed pawn on the h-file. The line starts with 4.Kf4 h4 5.Kf3: the white king retreats before blockading the pawn. The kings stand on f3 and h3, with g3 between them and Black to move. That lateral opposition stops the black king from getting through.

It is tempting to bring the king straight to the pawn. The attempt 4.Kg5?, however, loses: 4...h4! 5.Kf4 Kg2, and the black king gets in. The white retreat comes after the moment when the barrier needed to be ready. Being closer to the pawn does not mean defending it better.

In the line, 5...Kh2 6.Kf2 keeps the lateral opposition. After 6...h3 the pawn controls g2, and 7.Kf1 prepares the defensive continuation without stepping onto that square. The fixed pawns on the a-file give Black no reserve with which to undo that coordination.

In the next part, the same question about the turn will be applied to defending one’s own pawn. First check whether there is an immediate capture; then compare the defence before and after the opponent’s approach.
step.d_synchronize: Follow the kings’ ranks. Each retreat prepares useful opposition after the opponent’s reply.
step.d_synchronize.m1: 4.Kf4. The king retreats to coordinate the defense rather than racing directly toward the pawn.
step.d_synchronize.m2: 4...h4. The pawn advances and now controls g3.
step.d_synchronize.m3: 5.Kf3. The kings stand on f3 and h3. Black is to move: lateral opposition prevents the black king from crossing g3.
step.d_synchronize.m4: 5...Kh2. The black king drops to h2 to clear the way for the pawn and try to get out via g1. The white king follows with 6.Kf2, on the same rank, with g2 between the kings.
step.d_synchronize.m5: 6.Kf2. Lateral opposition reappears on f2 and h2, with Black to move.
step.d_synchronize.m6: 6...h3. The pawn advances again and controls g2. The defense must respect that attacked square.
step.d_synchronize.m7: 7.Kf1. The king retreats to the first rank. The continuation will show how to regain opposition and block the pawn.
step.d_synchronizeFinish: The defence continues until the passed pawn is captured. In this position Black is to move.
step.d_synchronizeFinish.m1: 7...Kg3. The black king reaches the g-file. The white king can respond on the same file.
step.d_synchronizeFinish.m2: 8.Kg1. The kings stand on g1 and g3, with Black to move: the opposition is now direct.
step.d_synchronizeFinish.m3: 8...Kf3. The black king leaves the g-file, allowing White to approach through h2.
step.d_synchronizeFinish.m4: 9.Kh2. The king blocks the pawn. The initial fixation and the sequence of oppositions made it possible to arrive in time.
step.d_synchronizeFinish.m5: 9...Ke3. The black king seeks activity on the other wing but can no longer prevent the capture on h3.
step.d_synchronizeFinish.m6: 10.Kxh3. The passed pawn has been eliminated. The position remains drawn; the a-pawns are still on the board.
step.synchronizeMove: Play White and find the best move. The black king, on h3, supports the h5-pawn.
step.synchronizeMove.hint:
Choose the retreat by the opposition it prepares, rather than just by proximity to the pawn. Respect the squares controlled by the pawn.

These do not work either:

At move 4
The approach through g5 and the deviation to e4 lose because they do not prepare the defense on the correct rank.
If White played 4.Ke4?, Black would reply 4...Kg3 and win. The line would be 4.Ke4 Kg3 5.Kd3 h4.
If White played 4.Kg5?, Black would reply 4...h4 and win. The line would be 4.Kg5 h4 5.Kf4 Kg2.

At move 5
At this decision, moving away to e3 or up to g5 lets the black king enter through g3. Lateral opposition must prevent that passage.
If White played 5.Ke3?, Black would reply 5...Kg3 and win. The line would be 5.Ke3 Kg3 6.Kd2 h3.
If White played 5.Kg5?, Black would reply 5...Kg3 and win. The line would be 5.Kg5 Kg3 6.Kf5 h3.

At move 6
The black king has changed rank. Moving upward again fails to follow that change and allows the pawn to advance with support.
If White played 6.Kg4?, Black would reply 6...h3 and win. The line would be 6.Kg4 h3 7.Kf3 Kg1.

At move 7
The pawn controls g2. Returning to the third rank abandons the defense along the first; the black king can support the next advance.
If White played 7.Kf3?, Black would reply 7...Kg1 and win. The line would be 7.Kf3 Kg1 8.Ke3 h2.
step.synchronizeMove.done:
Defence in step: the white king follows along the correct rank, alternating lateral and direct opposition until the pawn is stopped. The initial fixation made this coordination possible. In another structure, the purpose of fixation may require a different order.

The main line is 4.Kf4 h4 5.Kf3 Kh2 6.Kf2 h3 7.Kf1.
step.err_fixedTarget: White has just moved the king to e6, starting the race before fixing a5. See how Black uses the distant advance and preserves the win.
step.err_fixedTarget.m1: 1...a4. Black uses the advance that fixation would have prevented.
step.err_fixedTarget.m2: 2.Kd5. The white king seeks a central defense, but the position is already lost against correct play.
step.err_fixedTarget.m3: 2...h5. The other pawn advances too. White must cope with resources on both wings.
step.err_fixedTarget.m4: 3.Kd4. The king continues its approach; activity alone does not restore the draw.
step.err_fixedTarget.m5: 3...Kg3. Black attacks h3 with a winning position. The order of fixation and the king’s approach was decisive.
step.err_synchronize: White has just moved the king to g5, bringing it closer without preparing the defensive rank. See how the pawn advances with support from the black king.
step.err_synchronize.m1: 4...h4. The pawn gains space while the white king is still on the fifth rank.
step.err_synchronize.m2: 5.Kf4. The white king retreats but has not reached the third rank when lateral opposition would be needed.
step.err_synchronize.m3: 5...Kg2. The black king reaches the second rank and preserves the win. The approach through g5 did not prevent this entry.
step.err_synchronize.m4: 6.Ke3. The white king tries to return to the defense but has not recovered an effective barrier.
step.err_synchronize.m5: 6...h3. The pawn advances supported by the king on g2. Black remains winning: coordination was lost before this approach.
step.t_fixedTarget.hint3:
Starting the king’s race leaves Black the a-file reserve. Even when it is not used immediately, its availability changes the coordination of the defense. Prepare the structure before the route.

If White played 1.Kc6?, Black would reply 1...Kg3 and win. The line would be 1.Kc6 Kg3 2.Kb5 Kxh3.

If White played 1.Kd6?, Black would reply 1...Kg3 and win. The line would be 1.Kd6 Kg3 2.Ke5 Kxh3.

If White played 1.Ke6?, Black would reply 1...a4 and win. The line would be 1.Ke6 a4 2.Kd5 h5.
step.t_synchronize.hint3:
Being closer to the pawn or seeking the center is not enough. These deviations fail to prepare the rank on which the king must face its opponent after the advance.

If White played 4.Ke4?, Black would reply 4...Kg3 and win. The line would be 4.Ke4 Kg3 5.Kd3 h4.

If White played 4.Kg5?, Black would reply 4...h4 and win. The line would be 4.Kg5 h4 5.Kf4 Kg2.
step.t_carlsenSo.hint3: Stepping sideways abandons the opposition relationship and allows the white king to advance with its pawns. Both 55...Ke5 56.Ke3 Kd5 57.Kf4 and 55...Kg6 56.Ke4 Kf6 57.Kd5 leave White with a winning position. Consider how to preserve the distance before contesting lateral space.
step.t_euwe.hint3: Advancing the pawn or approaching through the center does not settle the race between the two targets: 49.c3 Ke4 50.Kb3 Kd3 and 49.Kd5 a4 50.Kc4 Ke4 lead to drawn positions. Compare the kings’ ranks and the route to a5 before choosing the advance.
step.t_lesson.hint3:
Advancing the pawn early or approaching with the king on the wrong file lets the defender maintain the barrier. Compare the key square each move prepares.

If White played 1.Ke3?, Black would reply 1...Ke7 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.Ke3 Ke7 2.g4 Ke6.

If White played 1.g4?, Black would reply 1...Kd7 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.g4 Kd7 2.g5 Kd6.
step.t_diagonal.hint3:
Advancing the pawn without support or approaching through the apparently most direct square does not guarantee a key square. The black king can reorganize the opposition.

If White played 1.e4?, Black would reply 1...Ke5 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.e4 Ke5 2.Ke2 Kxe4.

If White played 1.Ke4?, Black would reply 1...Ke6 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.Ke4 Ke6 2.Kd3 Kd5.
step.t_capablanca.hint3:
Stepping sideways before restricting the opposing king allows it to follow. The change of target must be prepared through the contest for opposition.

If White played 1.Kd2?, Black would reply 1...Kf7 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.Kd2 Kf7 2.Kc3 Ke6.

If White played 1.Kf2?, Black would reply 1...Kd7 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.Kf2 Kd7 2.Ke3 Ke7.
step.t_outflank.hint3:
Switching early to the queenside leaves the black king counterplay against h4. Restrict that access before going around.

If White played 4.Kd4?, Black would reply 4...Kf5 and hold the draw. The line would be 4.Kd4 Kf5 5.Kc5 Kg4.

If White played 4.Kd5?, Black would reply 4...Kf5 and hold the draw. The line would be 4.Kd5 Kf5 5.Kd4 Kf4.
step.t_edge.hint3:
Approaching without preparing opposition or retreating toward the center lets the black king continue blocking the entry. Compare access to the target after Black’s reply.

If White played 1.Kd6?, Black would reply 1...Kb6 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.Kd6 Kb6 2.Ke5 Ka7.

If White played 1.Ke4?, Black would reply 1...Ka6 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.Ke4 Ka6 2.Kd3 Ka5.
step.t_edgeCorner.hint3:
An immediate approach lets Black follow along the edge. A waiting move must prepare a relationship between the kings that forces the defender to give way.

If White played 1.Ke6?, Black would reply 1...Ka6 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.Ke6 Ka6 2.Ke5 Ka7.

If White played 1.Ke7?, Black would reply 1...Ka7 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.Ke7 Ka7 2.Kd6 Kb6.
step.t_waiting.hint3:
Moving the king too early leaves Black a useful pawn advance; spending both pawn advances also lets Black draw. Before approaching, compare both sides’ reserves.

If White played 1.Kb8?, Black would reply 1...b4 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.Kb8 b4 2.cxb4 Kb5.

If White played 1.b4?, Black would reply 1...Ka6 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.b4 Ka6 2.Kb8 Kb6.
step.t_useReserve.hint3:
Advancing the pawn before capturing the blocker gives time for captures on the other wing. Compare the king’s route with the pawn advance: the two actions have different effects.

If White played 4.h6?, Black would reply 4...Kxc4 and hold the draw. The line would be 4.h6 Kxc4 5.b3+ Kxb3.
step.t_means.hint3:
An unsupported advance lets the opposing king catch and capture the pawn. First organize the squares that make promotion possible.

If White played 1.c5?, Black would reply 1...Kd7 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.c5 Kd7 2.c6+ Kxc6.
step.t_means.hint2: A key square lets the king support the pawn’s advance even against the best defense. Compare that goal with merely maintaining the confrontation between the kings.
step.d_capablancaReturn: The kings are on d3 and e7, as in the practice after Black’s second move, and White is to move. The white king should not go up at once: first it regains the opposition on the file to which the black king returned.
step.d_capablancaReturn.m1: 3.Ke3! The king moves along the rank and leaves three squares between the kings on the e-file, with Black to move. This is the only move that preserves the win. If White advanced directly, Black would draw: 3.Kd4 Kd6 4.Ke4 Ke6 returns direct opposition to Black; 3.Ke4 Ke6 4.Kd4 Kf5 lets the black king approach h4.
step.d_capablancaReturn.m2: 3...Ke6. The black king reduces the distance. There are now two squares between the kings, and White can respond on the same axis.
step.d_capablancaReturn.m3: 4.Ke4! With the kings on e4 and e6 and Black to move, White takes direct opposition. The position remains winning: the lateral waiting move prepared an effective approach rather than merely adding a step toward the pawns.
part.protectPawn.title: Protecting the pawn
part.protectPawn.summary: Lateral opposition keeps your own pawn protected when the move order is coordinated.
step.t_protectPawn: The black king is on b6 and protects c6; the white king on e7 wants to capture that pawn. The pawns are blocked. How can Black prepare a defence that still works after White’s approach?
step.t_protectPawn.hint1: Before moving closer to the pawn, check whether White can capture it immediately.
step.t_protectPawn.hint2: The pawn provides no waiting move. Look for a relationship between the kings that makes the attacker give way.
step.t_protectPawn.hint3: Compare the kings’ rank after your move and who will be able to answer the next approach.
step.d_protectPawn: Watch when c6 comes under attack and how the black king adjusts the opposition without having to abandon the defence.
step.d_protectPawn.m1: 1...Ka7. The wait leaves three squares between the kings on the seventh rank and gives White the move; c6 cannot yet be captured.
step.d_protectPawn.m2: 2.Kd7. The attacker approaches c6. The defence must now shorten the distance without giving away the favourable move order.
step.d_protectPawn.m3: 2...Kb7. The black king faces the white king on d7, with c7 between them and White to move. It also protects c6 directly.
step.d_protectPawn.m4: 3.Kd6. The white king changes ranks to renew the attack on c6. Leaving the black king on its previous square is not enough.
step.d_protectPawn.m5: 3...Kb6. The black king follows on the sixth rank and protects c6; White has to move. Keep this picture: kings on b6 and d6, with the attacker to move.
step.err_protectPawn: In this position, after 1...Kc7?, the black king moved closer to its own pawn, but now Black loses. Follow White’s reply and compare, at the end, who is to move with the earlier defence.
step.err_protectPawn.m1: 2.Ke6. The white king reaches the sixth rank; Black’s own c6-pawn prevents its king from occupying that square to obtain lateral opposition.
step.err_protectPawn.m2: 2...Kb7. The black king still protects c6, but no longer coordinates the move order as in the correct defence. Even so, there is a common trap for White: the natural 3.Kd6? attacks c6, but 3...Kb6! leaves the kings on b6 and d6 with White to move, and Black draws. 3.Kd7 or 3.Kf7 wins, leaving Black to move.
step.err_protectPawn.m3: 3.Kd7. The attacker reaches the same rank, with c7 between the kings and Black to move. Direct protection does not solve the need to make a move.
step.err_protectPawn.m4: 3...Kb6. The defender changes ranks and still guards c6; White can answer that change.
step.err_protectPawn.m5: 4.Kd6. The kings are again on b6 and d6, but Black now moves. The blocked pawns provide no waiting move; the defender must give way.
step.err_protectPawn.m6: 4...Ka7. In this continuation, the black king abandons the defence of c6. Moving away makes the effect of the unfavourable move order visible.
step.err_protectPawn.m7:
5.Kxc6. Compare the pictures with the kings on b6 and d6: in the correct defence, White was to move; in the wrong line, Black had to give way because the pawns provided no waiting move.

Before choosing the defence, check for an immediate capture. If waiting is possible, follow the attacker’s reply and the black king’s adjustment. In the resulting position, who will be to move and have to abandon the protection? That comparison determines whether bringing the king closer helps.
step.protectPawnMove.hint: Keep c6 defended by coordinating the kings’ rank and the move order. Answer each approach; do not simply choose the square nearest the pawn.
step.protectPawnMove.done: The wait 1...Ka7 prepared the defence: after each approach, your king reached the direct protection of c6 with White to move.
step.d_edgeCorner.m4: 2...Kb7. The black king shortens the distance and keeps protecting c6. Now White looks for the passage that will force it to move again.
step.d_edgeCorner.m5: 3.Kd7! The white king enters along the seventh rank, attacks c6 and leaves Black to move. Going straight to d6 would allow 3...Kb6!, with the opposition on the same rank for Black.
step.d_edgeCorner.m6: 3...Kb6. The black king protects c6 along the sixth rank. White now replies, so the approach can continue with the favourable move order.
step.d_edgeCorner.m7: 4.Kd6. The defender must move and has no pawn waiting move. Compare the two targets, c6 and c5, before choosing the next capture.
step.d_edgeCornerCapture: Going round has reached the useful point: Black has to give up the defence of one of the pawns. Watch which pawn comes within reach after this reply.
step.d_edgeCornerCapture.m1: 4...Ka5. The black king has left b6 and left c5 unprotected. In the capture, what also counts is the square from which the white king protects its own c4-pawn.
step.d_edgeCornerCapture.m2: 5.Kxc5. The white king captures on c5, keeps the pressure on c6 and stops the black king from crossing b4 and b5. The initial waiting move has turned into a concrete gain of material.
step.protectPawn:
Now the opposition must keep a black pawn, the one on c6. The white king on e7 cannot capture it yet: it first has to come closer. That gives Black time to prepare the defence instead of rushing next to the pawn.

The waiting move 1...Ka7 draws. The kings stand on the seventh rank with three squares between them and White to move. After 2.Kd7, Black replies 2...Kb7; after 3.Kd6, it replies 3...Kb6. The black king follows the attacker’s rank and keeps c6 protected.

The approach 1...Kc7? seems to reinforce c6, but loses after 2.Ke6! In the line of the mistake, the kings also reach b6 and d6; the difference is that Black has to move. Because the pawns are blocked, the king has to give up the defence of one of the pawns.

Always compare the two pictures: the protection now and the protection after the reply. The waiting move only helps when it allows no immediate capture and sets up the right turn to follow the attacker.
step.d_secondReserve.m6: 3...Kd4. The black king approaches c4 but leaves the defence of the kingside. The reserve has been spent: now compare Black’s counterplay with the available entry beside h7.
step.d_secondReserve.m7:
4.Kh6 threatens h7. The c-pawn reserve has done its job: it gave Black the move without taking the white king away from the target. After 3...Kd4, the defender approached c4 but left the entry on h6.

Before waiting again, state what that wait would achieve. Here the new plan is to capture h7 and free h5; compare that gain with Black’s attack on c4. Another wait only makes sense if it preserves the position’s objective.
step.protectPawnMove: Play Black and find the best move. The white king on e7 cannot capture c6 yet.
step.intro.alt.g4: After this advance, Black finds a resource: the white king is not on a key square yet, and the black king gains time to stand in front of the pawn.
step.intro.alt.g4.m2: This move holds the draw. The black king stands in front of the pawn, and the white king can no longer reach a key square.
step.convert.alt.g4: With this advance you let the win slip: the white king is one step from the key square, but the pawn goes first, and the black king gains time to stand in front of it.

step.capablanca.alt.kf3.m2: This move holds the draw: the kings face each other on the f-file. With three squares between them and White to move, the opposition passes to Black.

step.capablancaMove.alt.kf3.m2: This move takes the distant opposition: three squares between the kings, f4, f5 and f6, and White to move.

step.convert.r1: The black king goes to the e-file and faces your king, with three squares between them.
step.convert.r2: The black king goes to f7, on its way to the front of the pawn.
step.diagonalMove.r1: The black king moves up to d5 and tries to approach the e3-pawn.
step.defendMove.r1: The white king moves up to e4, looking to enter via d5 or f5.
step.defendMove.r2: White advances the pawn and passes the move to you.
step.lateralDefend.r1: The white king heads back to the centre along the fifth rank, to support the d2-pawn.
step.lateralDefend.r2: The white king drops to b4, still on its way to the d2-pawn.
step.capablancaMove.r1: 1...Kf8. The black king steps to the f-file, looking for another square from which to take the opposition. This is a common trap: the natural 2.Ke3? seems to keep the king in the centre, but after 2...Ke7! the kings stand on e3 and e7, with three squares between them and White to move, and Black draws with the distant opposition. What wins is 2.Kd3 or 2.Kf2: if the black king returns to e7, the white king steps onto e3 right after, and the opposition belongs to White.
step.capablancaMove.r2: 2...Ke7. The black king returns to the e-file, trying to face your king again. Another common trap: the natural 3.Kd4? seems to advance, but 3...Kd6! puts the kings face to face on the d-file, with one square between them and White to move, and Black draws. What wins is 3.Ke3: three squares between the kings on the e-file, and Black to move.
step.outflankMove.r1: The black king goes to g6 to protect the h5-pawn.
step.reserveMove.r1: The black king advances to e6 and stays on the e-file, facing your king.
step.reserveMove.r2: The black king advances one more square, to e5, and tries to reach the white pawns.
step.edgeMove.r1: 1...Ka6. The black king moves up to a6, because it cannot stay on the fifth rank: b5 is covered by the c4-pawn. Watch out for a common trap: the natural 2.Ke5? seems to bring the king closer, but Black replies 2...Kb7! (or 2...Ka7) and draws. 2.Ke6 or 2.Kg6 wins: the white king moves up to the sixth rank and takes the distant opposition, with Black to move.
step.edgeMove.r2: The black king goes to b6 to protect the c6- and c5-pawns.
step.edgeCornerMove.r1: The black king retreats to a7 and waits, without losing contact with b6.
step.edgeCornerMove.r2: The black king goes to b7 and protects the c6-pawn again.
step.grigorievMove.r1: The black king goes to a5 and waits beside the b5-pawn.
step.grigorievMove.r2: Black advances the pawn to b4, to attack c3 and change the move.
step.secondReserveMove.r1: The black king goes to e4, to approach the centre and the white pawns.
step.secondReserveMove.r2: The black king advances to e5, eyeing the queenside pawns, while the h7-pawn stops your king from going through g6.
step.useReserveMove.r1: The black king goes to d3, on its way to the c4-pawn.
step.useReserveMove.r2: The black king captures the c4-pawn and prepares the advance of the c5-pawn.
step.fixedTargetMove.r1: The black king goes to g3 to attack the h3-pawn.
step.fixedTargetMove.r2: The black king captures the h3-pawn and clears the way for the h6-pawn.
step.synchronizeMove.r1: Black advances the pawn to h4, trying to push it through.
step.synchronizeMove.r2: The black king goes to h2, looking to enter via g1 or g2.
step.synchronizeMove.r3: The pawn advances to h3 and now controls g2.
step.protectPawnMove.r1: The white king goes to d7 to attack the c6-pawn.
step.protectPawnMove.r2: The white king drops to d6 and attacks the c6-pawn again, now also close to c5.
step.meansMove.r1: The black king retreats to d7, trying to get in front of the pawn.
step.intro.short: With 1.Ke4!, three squares lie between the kings, e5, e6 and e7, and Black is to move: White has the distant opposition. If the black king goes to f7 or f8, you answer 2.Kf5!, and the white king reaches the key square before the pawn advances.
step.diagonal.short: With 1.Kf4!, the kings stand on the diagonal with one square between them, e5, and Black is to move. After 1...Ke6, you answer 2.Ke4!, face to face, and Black must give way. 1.Ke4? Ke6 would give Black the direct opposition.
step.defend.short: In Carlsen–So (Stavanger, 2017), 55...Kf7! left three squares between the kings, f4, f5 and f6, with White to move. When the white king changed file, Black followed: 56.Ke3 Ke7 57.Kd3 Kd7. The distant opposition also serves the defender.
step.lateral.short: Euwe played 49.Kb5: the king attacks the a5-pawn and stands on the fifth rank, with three squares between the kings and Black to move. This is the distant opposition along the rank; after capturing a5, the white king returns close to the c2-pawn.
step.capablanca.short: With six squares between the kings, an even number, the side to move takes the opposition: 1.Ke2! is the only winning move. After 1...Ke7, only 2.Ke3! keeps it: three squares between the kings and Black to move. Whoever has the opposition reaches the opponent's pawn first.
step.outflank.short: Outflanking means going through the wing the enemy king has left free. 4.Kf4 keeps the opposition and protects the approach to h4; after 4...Kg6, 5.Ke5 switches the target to the b5-pawn.
step.reserve.short: A reserve is a pawn move that changes the move without moving the kings. 1.a3 leaves the kings on e1 and e7, and it is Black to move. After 1...Ke6 2.Ke2 Ke5 3.Ke3, the white king has the direct opposition. Here 1.Ke2 also wins.
step.edge.short: After 1.Kd6? Kb6!, c6 lies between the kings with White to move: a draw. The right idea is to step away: 1.Kf5! The black king cannot stay on the fifth rank, because b5 is covered by the c4-pawn; it moves up, and the white king moves up with it.
step.edgeCorner.short: 1.Ke8 Ka7 2.Ke7 leaves three squares between the kings on the seventh rank, with Black to move. After 2...Kb7, 3.Kd7! uses d7 as a passage; after 3...Kb6 4.Kd6, the black king must give way. 3.Kd6? Kb6! leaves White to move, and it is a draw.
step.waiting.short: After 1.b3 Ka5, 2.Kb8! waits with the king. The approach 2.Ka7? b4 3.c4 leaves Black with no legal move and not in check: stalemate, a draw. In the right line, 2...b4 3.c4 passes the move with the white king still at a distance.
step.secondReserve.short: A pawn on the second rank can give two tempi, one square at a time. The line 1.c3 Ke4 2.Kg5 Ke5 saves the advance to c4: 3.c4 changes the move with the white king close to h7. 3.h6? only draws, because Black answers 3...c4.
step.useReserve.short: 4.Kh6 reaches the blocker from the front, without going through g6, which the h7-pawn controls. After 4...Kd3, 5.Kxh7 removes it; even after 5...Kxc4, 6.h6 keeps the win. Now the pawn advance serves promotion.
step.fixedTarget.short: 1.a4! is the only drawing move: it fixes the a5-pawn and takes from Black a reserve that would change the move during the defence. After 1...Kg3 2.Ke6 Kxh3 3.Kf5, White has given up h3 but keeps a defensive route.
step.synchronize.short: With 4.Kf4 h4 5.Kf3, the white king retreats before blocking the pawn: the kings stand on f3 and h3, with g3 between them and Black to move. This sideways opposition stops the black king. 4.Kg5? loses: 4...h4! 5.Kf4 Kg2, and the black king gets in.
step.protectPawn.short: The waiting move 1...Ka7 draws: the kings stand on the seventh rank with three squares between them and White to move. After 2.Kd7 Kb7 3.Kd6 Kb6, the black king keeps pace and keeps c6 protected. 1...Kc7? loses after 2.Ke6!
step.means.short: 1.Ke4 takes the opposition but only draws after 1...Kd6. 1.Kc5! wins because it brings the king closer to the key squares b6, c6 and d6; after 1...Kd7, 2.Kb6 reaches one of them. The opposition only counts if it helps to promote or capture.
ex.e09.r1: 1...Kf7. The black king leaves the g-file and heads for the centre, towards e6 and d5, in front of the d2-pawn. If the white king does not follow it with the distant opposition on the new file, Black takes it, and the pawn does not get through.
ex.e11.r1: 2.Kd2. The white king changes file, heading for c3 and d3, from where it threatens to reach the key squares of the c2-pawn: b4, c4 and d4. Ask yourself on which square your king keeps the opposition after this change.
ex.e11.r2: 3.Kd3. The white king climbs to the third rank; from d3, one step takes it to c4 or d4, two key squares. There is no room left for the distant opposition: now it has to be direct.
ex.e11.r3: 4.Kc3. The white king tries from the side: from c3, it aims at b4 and c4. If your king does not stand face to face with it, a key square falls.
ex.e13.r1: 1...Kd2. The black king attacks the e3-pawn and looks for a way in through e2. Your king must defend e3 without giving up the opposition along the rank.
ex.e13.r2: 2...Kd3. The black king moves up and attacks e3 from the other side; now the entry it is looking for is e4. The idea is the same: follow it on its rank, with one square between the kings and Black to move.
ex.e14.r1: 1...Kc3. The black king attacks the c2-pawn and keeps the d5-pawn in reserve, a move to change the turn whenever it suits Black. The white king has to protect c2 again.
ex.e14.r2: 2...Kb4. The black king retreats to b4, still holding the d5 reserve. This is a common trap: the natural 3.Kb2? takes the direct opposition, but 3...d4! passes the move, and you are the one who must give way; Black draws. 3.Kc1, 3.Ka1 or 3.Ka2 wins: the white king waits without spending the opposition too early.
ex.e14.r3: 3...Kc3. The black king returns to c3 and attacks c2 again. Black repeats the manoeuvre hoping for a slip; c2 is still protected, and the white king must keep answering without giving up the opposition.
ex.e14.r4: 4...d4. Black spends the reserve: the pawn advances and threatens to go on to d3 to trade off the c2-pawn. Now Black has no waiting move left.
ex.e14.r5: 5...d3. The pawn attacks c2 and forces the trade. After it, everything is decided by the kings' race for the b3-pawn.
ex.e14.r6: 6...Kxd3. The black king recaptures and aims at the b3-pawn. The win depends on the white king protecting b3 in time and then escorting the pawn.
ex.e15.r1: 1...Ke3. The black king runs towards d2 to attack the c2-pawn. This is a common trap: the natural 2.Kf5? takes the king to the centre, but 2...Kd2! attacks c2, and Black draws. What wins is 2.c3: the pawn advances one square before the black king arrives, and the second step, c4, is kept in reserve.
ex.e15.r2: 2...Ke4. The black king stands on the same rank as yours, with one square between them and White to move: this is the opposition along the rank, which stops the white king from advancing through the centre. White, however, still has the move c3-c4 in hand.
ex.e15.r3: 3...Ke5. The black king moves up as well and keeps the opposition along the rank; if the white king steps towards the centre, it answers face to face.
ex.e15.r4: 4...Ke6. One more step up, again with one square between the kings and White to move. The opposition is still Black's, but the room to climb is running out.
ex.e15.r5: 5...Ke7. The kings reach the seventh rank, with Black still holding the opposition. The black king has nowhere left to climb; think about how to change the turn without moving the kings.
ex.e15.r6: 6...Ke6. The reserve has been spent, and the black king turns towards the c4-pawn, by way of e5 and d4. This is a common trap: the natural 7.Kg6? faces the black king again, but 7...Ke5! goes on to d4, the c4-pawn falls, and Black draws. What wins is 7.Kf8: the white king goes round behind and returns to the centre along the e-file in time.
ex.e15.r7: 7...Ke5. The black king runs to d4, from where it will attack the c4-pawn. The white king has to return to the centre with gain of tempo; remember that the b2-pawn can still protect c4.
ex.e16.r1: 1...Kd7. The black king sets off for the queenside, to go round via c6 and d5 and attack the e5-pawn. Your king has another target, the h7-pawn, and must march there in step with the black king.
ex.e16.r2: 2...Kc6. The black king continues its detour, now heading for d5. With h7 fixed as the target, the white king heads for the kingside; each of its squares must correspond to the black king's square.
ex.e16.r3: 3...Kd5. The black king stands next to the e5-pawn and could already capture it. It prefers to wait, because the capture only wins if the white king is on a square that does not correspond to its own.
ex.e16.r4: 4...Kd4. The black king makes a waiting step, without capturing. It tests whether the white king knows the square that corresponds to d4; one move out of step, and capturing on e5 wins.
ex.e16.r5: 5...Ke4. Another waiting step, now to e4, still next to the e5-pawn. Once again, the white king must find the square that corresponds to this one.
ex.e16.r6: 6...Kxe5. At last the black king captures the e5-pawn and wants to go on to f6, towards h7, to defend it. The white king must block that path with the opposition.
